entries.a5ea3a7ea844b8b3ac7707098a9e6954f2bb92e8: <div sID="gen4366" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Josh.13" sID="Josh.13"/> <div eID="gen4366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4367" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4368" type="x-p"/> At this chapter begins the account of the dividing of the land of Canaan among the tribes of Israel by lot, a narrative not so entertaining and instructive as that of the conquest of it, and yet it is thought fit to be inserted in the sacred history, to illustrate the performance of the promise made to the fathers, that this land should be given to the seed of Jacob, to them and not to any other. The preserving of this distribution would be of great use to the Jewish nation, who were obliged by the law to keep up this first distribution, and not to transfer inheritances from tribe to tribe, <reference osisRef="Num.36.9">Num. xxxvi. 9</reference>. It is likewise of use to us for the explaining of other scriptures: the learned know how much light the geographical description of a country gives to the history of it. And therefore we are not to skip over these chapters of hard names as useless and not to be regarded; where God has a mouth to speak and a hand to write we should find an ear to hear an eye to read; and God give us a heart to profit! In this chapter, I. God informs Joshua what parts of the country that were intended in the grant to Israel yet remained unconquered, and not got in possession, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.1-Josh.13.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. He appoints him, notwithstanding, to make a distribution of what was conquered, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.7">ver. 7</reference>. III. To complete this account, here is a repetition of the distribution Moses had made of the land on the other side Jordan; in general (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.8-Josh.13.14">ver. 8-14</reference>), in particular, the lot of Reuben (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.15-Josh.13.23">ver. 15-23</reference>), of Gad (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.24-Josh.13.28">ver. 24-28</reference>), of the half tribe of Manasseh, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.29-Josh.13.33">ver. 29-33</reference>.
entries.17e3455284456bcc8c0b3ef1bbffbcc0802912c2: <div eID="gen4368" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4367" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Distribution of Canaan. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1445.)</title> <div sID="gen4369" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now Joshua was old <hi type="italic">and</hi> stricken in years; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto him, Thou art old <hi type="italic">and</hi> stricken in years, and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed. <hi type="super">2</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the land that yet remaineth: all the borders of the Philistines, and all Geshuri, <hi type="super">3</hi> From Sihor, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> before Egypt, even unto the borders of Ekron northward, <hi type="italic">which</hi> is counted to the Canaanite: five lords of the Philistines; the Gazathites, and the Ashdothites, the Eshkalonites, the Gittites, and the Ekronites; also the Avites: <hi type="super">4</hi> From the south, all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that <hi type="italic">is</hi> beside the Sidonians, unto Aphek, to the borders of the Amorites: <hi type="super">5</hi> And the land of the Giblites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrising, from Baalgad under mount Hermon unto the entering into Hamath. <hi type="super">6</hi> All the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon unto Misrephothmaim, <hi type="italic">and</hi> all the Sidonians, them will I drive out from before the children of Israel: only divide thou it by lot unto the Israelites for an inheritance, as I have commanded thee. <div eID="gen4369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4370" type="x-p"/> Here, I. God puts Joshua in mind of his old age, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. It is said that Joshua was <hi type="italic">old and stricken in years,</hi> and he and Caleb were at this time the only old men among the thousands of Israel, none except them of all those who were numbered at Mount Sinai being now alive. He had been a man of war from his youth (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.10">Exod. xvii. 10</reference>); but now he yielded to the infirmities of age, with which it is in vain for the stoutest to think of contesting. It should seem Joshua had not the same strength and vigour in his old age that Moses had; all that come to old age do not find it alike good; generally, the days of old age are evil days, and such as there is no pleasure in, nor expectation of service from. 2. God takes notice of it to him: <hi type="italic">God said to him, Thou art old.</hi> Note, It is good for those who are <hi type="italic">old and stricken in years</hi> to be put in remembrance of their being so. Some have <hi type="italic">gray hairs here and there upon them, and perceive it not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.9">Hos. vii. 9</reference>); they do not care to think of it, and therefore need to be told of it, that they may be quickened to do the work of life, and make preparation for death, which is coming towards them apace. But God mentions Joshua's age and growing infirmities, (1.) As a reason why he should now lay by the thoughts of pursuing the war; he cannot expect to see an end of it quickly, for there remained much land, more perhaps than he thought, to be possessed, in several parts remote from each other: and it was not fit that at his age he should be put upon the fatigue of renewing the war, and carrying it to such distant places; no, it was enough for him that he had reduced the body of the country. "Let him be gathered to rest with honour and the thanks of his people for the good services he had done them, and let the conquering of the skirts of the country be left for those that shall come after." As he had entered into the labours of Moses, so let others enter into his, and bring forth the top-stone, the doing of which was reserved for David long after. Observe, God considers the frame of his people, and would not have them burdened with work above their strength. It cannot be expected that old people should do as they have done for God and their country. (2.) As a reason why he should speedily apply himself to the dividing of that which he had conquered. That work must be done, and done quickly; it was necessary that he should preside in the doing of it, and therefore, he being <hi type="italic">old and stricken in years,</hi> and not likely to continue long, let him make this his concluding piece of service to God and Israel. All people, but especially old people, should set themselves to do that quickly which must be done before they die, lest death prevent them, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">Eccl. ix. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen4370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4371" type="x-p"/> II. He gives him a particular account of the land that yet remained unconquered, which was intended for Israel, and which, in due time, they should be masters of if they did not put a bar in their own door. Divers places are here mentioned, some in the south, as the country of the Philistines, governed by five lords, and the land that lay towards Egypt (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.2-Josh.13.3">v. 2, 3</reference>), some westward, as that which lay towards the Sidonians (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.4">v. 4</reference>), some eastward, as all Lebanon (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.5">v. 5</reference>), some towards the north, as that in the entering in of Hamath, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.5">v. 5</reference>. Joshua is told this, and he made the people acquainted with it, 1. That they might be the more affected with God's goodness to them in giving them this good land, and might thereby be engaged to love and serve him; for, if this which they had was too little, God would moreover <hi type="italic">give them such and such things,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.8">2 Sam. xii. 8</reference>. 2. That they might not be tempted to make any league, or contract any dangerous familiarity with these their neighbours so as to learn their way, but might rather be jealous of them, as a people that kept them from their right and that they had just cause of quarrel with. 3. That they might keep themselves in a posture for war, and not think of putting off the harness so long as there remained any land to be possessed. Nor must we lay aside our spiritual armour, nor be off our watch, till our victory be completed in the kingdom of glory. <div eID="gen4371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4372" type="x-p"/> III. He promises that he would make the Israelites masters of all those countries that were yet unsubdued, though Joshua was old and not able to do it, old and not likely to live to see it done. Whatever becomes of us, and however we may be laid aside as despised broken vessels, God will do his own work in his own time (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will drive them out.</hi> The original is emphatic: "<hi type="italic">It is I that will do it,</hi> I that can do it when thou are dead and gone, and will do it if Israel be not wanting to themselves." "I will do it by my Word," so the Chaldee here, as in many other places, "by the eternal Word, the captain of the hosts of the Lord." This promise that he would drive them out from before the children of Israel plainly supposes it as the condition of the promise that the children of Israel must themselves attempt their extirpation, must go up against them, else they could not be said to be driven out before them; if afterwards Israel, through sloth, or cowardice, or affection to these idolaters, sit still and let them alone, they must blame themselves, and not God, if they be not driven out. We must work out our salvation, and then God will work in us and work with us; we must resist our spiritual enemies, and then God will tread them under our feet; we must go forth to our Christian work and warfare, and then God will go forth before us.
entries.a5e006a7f7686c7a5e8087bedbfaac43599ecfca: <div eID="gen4372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4373" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance unto the nine tribes, and the half tribe of Manasseh, <hi type="super">8</hi> With whom the Reubenites and the Gadites have received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond Jordan eastward, <hi type="italic">even</hi> as Moses the servant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> gave them; <hi type="super">9</hi> From Aroer, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon the bank of the river Arnon, and the city that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the midst of the river, and all the plain of Medeba unto Dibon; <hi type="super">10</hi> And all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, which reigned in Heshbon, unto the border of the children of Ammon; <hi type="super">11</hi> And Gilead, and the border of the Geshurites and Maachathites, and all mount Hermon, and all Bashan unto Salcah; <hi type="super">12</hi> All the kingdom of Og in Bashan, which reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei, who remained of the remnant of the giants: for these did Moses smite, and cast them out. <hi type="super">13</hi> Nevertheless the children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites, nor the Maachathites: but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day. <hi type="super">14</hi> Only unto the tribe of Levi he gave none inheritance; the sacrifices of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel made by fire <hi type="italic">are</hi> their inheritance, as he said unto them. <hi type="super">15</hi> And Moses gave unto the tribe of the children of Reuben <hi type="italic">inheritance</hi> according to their families. <hi type="super">16</hi> And their coast was from Aroer, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> on the bank of the river Arnon, and the city that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the midst of the river, and all the plain by Medeba; <hi type="super">17</hi> Heshbon, and all her cities that <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the plain; Dibon, and Bamothbaal, and Bethbaalmeon, <hi type="super">18</hi> And Jahazah, and Kedemoth, and Mephaath, <hi type="super">19</hi> And Kirjathaim, and Sibmah, and Zarethshahar in the mount of the valley, <hi type="super">20</hi> And Bethpeor, and Ashdothpisgah, and Bethjeshimoth, <hi type="super">21</hi> And all the cities of the plain, and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, which reigned in Heshbon, whom Moses smote with the princes of Midian, Evi, and Rekem, and Zur, and Hur, and Reba, <hi type="italic">which were</hi> dukes of Sihon, dwelling in the country. <hi type="super">22</hi> Balaam also the son of Beor, the soothsayer, did the children of Israel slay with the sword among them that were slain by them. <hi type="super">23</hi> And the border of the children of Reuben was Jordan, and the border <hi type="italic">thereof.</hi> This <hi type="italic">was</hi> the inheritance of the children of Reuben after their families, the cities and the villages thereof. <hi type="super">24</hi> And Moses gave <hi type="italic">inheritance</hi> unto the tribe of Gad, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto the children of Gad according to their families. <hi type="super">25</hi> And their coast was Jazer, and all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the children of Ammon, unto Aroer that <hi type="italic">is</hi> before Rabbah; <hi type="super">26</hi> And from Heshbon unto Ramathmizpeh, and Betonim; and from Mahanaim unto the border of Debir; <hi type="super">27</hi> And in the valley, Betharam, and Bethnimrah, and Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, Jordan and <hi type="italic">his</hi> border, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto the edge of the sea of Chinnereth on the other side Jordan eastward. <hi type="super">28</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the inheritance of the children of Gad after their families, the cities, and their villages. <hi type="super">29</hi> And Moses gave <hi type="italic">inheritance</hi> unto the half tribe of Manasseh: and <hi type="italic">this</hi> was <hi type="italic">the possession</hi> of the half tribe of the children of Manasseh by their families. <hi type="super">30</hi> And their coast was from Mahanaim, all Bashan, all the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all the towns of Jair, which <hi type="italic">are</hi> in Bashan, threescore cities: <hi type="super">31</hi> And half Gilead, and Ashtaroth, and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan, <hi type="italic">were pertaining</hi> unto the children of Machir the son of Manasseh, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the one half of the children of Machir by their families. <hi type="super">32</hi> These <hi type="italic">are the countries</hi> which Moses did distribute for inheritance in the plains of Moab, on the other side Jordan, by Jericho, eastward. <hi type="super">33</hi> But unto the tribe of Levi Moses gave not <hi type="italic">any</hi> inheritance: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel <hi type="italic">was</hi> their inheritance, as he said unto them. <div eID="gen4373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4374" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. Orders given to Joshua to assign to each tribe its portion of this land, including that which was yet unsubdued, which must be brought into the lot, in a believing confidence that it should be conquered when Israel was multiplied so as to have occasion for it (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Now divide this land.</hi> Joshua thought all must be conquered before any must be divided. "No," said, God, "there is as much conquered as will serve your turn for the present; divide this, and make your best of it, and wait for the remainder hereafter." Note, We must take the comfort of what we have, though we cannot compass all we would have. Observe, <div eID="gen4374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4375" type="x-p"/> 1. The land must be divided among the several tribes, and they must not always live in common, as now they did. Which way soever a just property is acquired, it is the will of that God who has given the earth to the children of men that there should be such a thing, and that every man should know his own, and not invade that which is another's. The world must be governed, not by force, but right, by the law of equity, not of arms. <div eID="gen4375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4376" type="x-p"/> 2. That it must be divided for an inheritance, though they got it by conquest. (1.) The promise of it came to them as an inheritance from their fathers; the land of promise pertained to the children of promise, who were thus beloved for their fathers' sakes, and in performance of the covenant with them. (2.) The possession of it was to be transmitted by them, as an inheritance to their children. Frequently, what is got by force is soon lost again; but Israel, having an incontestable title to this land by the divine grant, might see it hereby secured as an inheritance to their seed after them, and that God kept this mercy for thousands. <div eID="gen4376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4377" type="x-p"/> 3. That Joshua must not divide it by his own will. Though he was a very wise, just, and good man, it must not be left to him to give what he pleased to each tribe; but he must do it by lot, which referred the matter wholly to God, and to his determination, for he it is that appoints the bounds of our habitation, and every man's judgment must proceed from him. But Joshua must preside in this affair, must manage this solemn appeal to Providence, and see that the lot was drawn fairly and without fraud, and that every tribe did acquiesce in it. The lot indeed <hi type="italic">causeth contention to cease,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.18">Prov. xviii. 18</reference>. But, if upon this lot any controversy should arise, Joshua by his wisdom and authority must determine it, and prevent any ill consequences of it. Joshua must have the honour of dividing the land, (1.) Because he had undergone the fatigue of conquering it: and when, through his hand, each tribe received its allotment, they would thereby be made the more sensible of their obligations to him. And what a pleasure must it needs be to a man of such a public spirit as Joshua was to see the people that were so dear to him eating of the labour of his hands! (2.) That he might be herein a type of Christ, who has not only conquered for us the gates of hell, but has opened to us the gates of heaven, and, having purchased the eternal inheritance for all believers, will in due time put them all in possession of it. <div eID="gen4377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4378" type="x-p"/> II. An account is here given of the distribution of the land on the other side Jordan among the Reubenites, and Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh. Observe, <div eID="gen4378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4379" type="x-p"/> 1. How this account is introduced. It comes in, (1.) As the reason why this land within Jordan must be divided only to the nine tribes and a half, because the other two and a half were already provided for. (2.) As a pattern to Joshua in the work he had now to do. He had seen Moses distribute that land, which would give him some aid in distributing this, and thence he might take his measure; only this was to be done by lot, but it should seem Moses did that himself, according to the wisdom given unto him. (3.) As an inducement to Joshua to hasten the dividing of this land, that the nine tribes and a half might not be kept any longer than was necessary out of their possession, since their brethren of the two tribes and a half were so well settled in theirs; and God their common Father would not have such a difference made between his children. <div eID="gen4379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4380" type="x-p"/> 2. The particulars of this account. <div eID="gen4380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4381" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is a general description of the country that was given to the two tribes and a half, <hi type="italic">which Moses gave them, even as Moses gave them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.13.8">v. 8</reference>. The repetition implies a ratification of the grant by Joshua. Moses settled this matter, and, as Moses settled it, so shall it rest; Joshua will not, under any pretence whatsoever, go about to alter it. And a reason is intimated why he would not, because Moses was the servant of the Lord, and acted in this matter by secret direction from him and was faithful as a servant. Here we have, [1.] The fixing of the boundaries of this country, by which they were divided from the neighbouring nations, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.9-Josh.13.12">v. 9</reference>, &c. Israel must know their own and keep to it, and may not, under pretence of their being God's peculiar people, encroach upon their neighbours, and invade their rights and properties, to which they had a good and firm title by providence, though not, as Israel, a title by promise. [2.] An exception of one part of this country from Israel's possession, though it was in their grant, namely, the Geshurites and the Maachathites, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.13">v. 13</reference>. They had not leisure to reduce all the remote and obscure corners of the country in Moses's time, and afterwards they had no mind to it, being easy with what they had. Thus those who are not straitened in God's promises are yet straitened in their own faith, and prayers, and endeavours. <div eID="gen4381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4382" type="x-p"/> (2.) A very particular account of the inheritances of these two tribes and a half, how they were separated from each other, and what cites, with the towns, villages, and fields, commonly known and reputed to be appurtenances to them, belonged to each tribe. This is very fully and exactly set down in order that posterity might, in reading this history, be the more affected with the goodness of God to their ancestors, when they found what a large and fruitful country, and what abundance of great and famous cities, he put them in possession of (God's grants look best when we descend to the particulars); and also that the limits of every tribe being punctually set down in this authentic record disputes might be prevented, and such contests between the tribes as commonly happen where boundaries have not been adjusted nor this matter brought to a certainty. And we have reason to think that the register here prescribed and published of the lot of each tribe was of great use to Israel in after-ages, was often appealed to, and always acquiesced in, for the determining of <hi type="italic">meum</hi> and <hi type="italic">tuum</hi>—<hi type="italic">mine</hi> and <hi type="italic">thine.</hi> <div eID="gen4382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4383" type="x-p"/> [1.] We have here the lot of the tribe of Reuben, Jacob's first-born, who, though he had lost the dignity and power which pertained to the birthright, yet, it seems, had the advantage of being first served. Perhaps those of that tribe had an eye to this in desiring to be seated on that side Jordan, that, since they could not expect the benefit of the best lot, they might have the credit of the first. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In the account of the lot of this tribe mention is made of the slaughter, 1. Of Sihon, king of the Amorites, who reigned in this country, and might have kept it and his life if he would have been neighbourly, and have suffered Israel to pass through his territories, but, by attempting to oppose them, justly brought ruin upon himself, <reference osisRef="Num.21.21-Num.21.25">Num. xxi. 21</reference>, &c. 2. Of the princes of Midian, who were slain afterwards in another war (<reference osisRef="Num.31.8">Num. xxxi. 8</reference>), and yet are here called <hi type="italic">dukes of Sihon,</hi> and are said to be <hi type="italic">smitten with him,</hi> because they were either tributaries to him, or, in his opposition to Israel, confederates with him, and hearty in his interests, and his fall made way for theirs not long after. 3. Of Balaam particularly, that would, if he could, have cursed Israel, and was soon after recompensed <hi type="italic">according to the wickedness of his endeavour</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.4">Ps. xxviii. 4</reference>), for he fell with those that set him on. This was recorded before (<reference osisRef="Num.31.8">Num. xxxi. 8</reference>), and is here repeated, because the defeating of Balaam's purpose to curse Israel was the turning of that curse into a blessing, and was such an instance of the power and goodness of God as was fit to be had in everlasting remembrance. See <reference osisRef="Mic.6.5">Mic. vi. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Within the lot of this tribe was that Mount Pisgah from the top of which Moses took his view of the earthly Canaan and his flight to the heavenly. And not far off thence Elijah was when he was fetched up to heaven in a chariot of fire. The separation of this tribe from the rest, by the river Jordan, was that which Deborah lamented; and the preference they gave to their private interests above the public was what she censured, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.15-Judg.5.16">Judg. v. 15, 16</reference>. In this tribe lay Heshbon and Sibmah, famed for their fruitful fields and vineyards. See <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8-Isa.16.9">Isa. xvi. 8, 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.47.32">Jer. xlvii. 32</reference>. This tribe, with that of Gad, was sorely shaken by Hazael king of Syria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.33">2 Kings x. 33</reference>), and afterwards dislodged and carried into captivity, twenty years before the general captivity of the ten tribes by the king of Assyria, <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.26">1 Chron. v. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen4383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4384" type="x-p"/> [2.] The lot of the tribe of Gad, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.24-Josh.13.28">v. 24-28</reference>. This lay north of Reuben's lot; the country of Gilead lay in this tribe, so famous for its balm that it is thought strange indeed if there be no balm in Gilead, and the cities of Jabesh-Gilead and Ramoth-Gilead which we often read of in scripture. Succoth and Penuel, which we read of in the story of Gideon, were in this tribe; and that forest which is called the <hi type="italic">wood of Ephraim</hi> (from the slaughter Jephthah made there of the Ephraimites), in which Absalom's rebellious army was beaten, while his father David lay at Mahanaim, one of the frontier-cities of this tribe, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.26">v. 26</reference>. Sharon, famous for roses, was in this tribe. And within the limits of this tribe lived those Gadarenes that loved their swine better than their Saviour, fitter to be called <hi type="italic">Girgashites</hi> than <hi type="italic">Israelites.</hi> <div eID="gen4384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4385" type="x-p"/> [3.] The lot of the half-tribe of Manasseh, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.29-Josh.13.31">v. 29-31</reference>. Bashan, the kingdom of Og, was in this allotment, famous for the best timber, witness the oaks of Bashan—and the best breed of cattle, witness the bulls and rams of Bashan. This tribe lay north of Gad, reached to Mount Hermon, and had in it part of Gilead. Mispeh was in this half-tribe, and Jephthah was one of its ornaments; so was Elijah, for in this tribe was Thisbe, whence he is called the Tishbite; and Jair was another. In the edge of the tribe stood Chorazin, honoured with Christ's wondrous works, but ruined by his righteous woe for not improving them. <div eID="gen4385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4386" type="x-p"/> [4.] Twice in this chapter it is taken notice of that to the tribe of Levi <hi type="italic">Moses gave no inheritance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.14">v. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.33">33</reference>), for so God had appointed, <reference osisRef="Num.18.20">Num. xviii. 20</reference>. If they had been appointed to a lot entire by themselves, Moses would have served them first, not because it was his own tribe, but because it was God's; but they must be provided for in another manner; their habitations must be scattered in all the tribes, and their maintenance brought out of all the tribes, and God himself was the portion both of their inheritance and of their cup, <reference osisRef="Deut.10.9">Deut. x. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.2">xviii. 2</reference>.  <chapter eID="Josh.13"/> <div eID="gen4386" type="x-p"/>

entries.45860e34bc553ba1fb0e1e76da18802f42e8ad0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2104"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.13.1-Josh.13.33">Jos 13:1-33</reference>. Bounds of the Land Not Yet Conquered.</title> <div sID="gen2822" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2104"/><hi type="bold">1. Now Joshua was old and stricken in years--</hi>He was probably above a hundred years old; for the conquest and survey of the land occupied about seven years, the partition one; and he died at the age of one hundred ten years (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.29">Jos 24:29</reference>). The distribution, as well as the conquest of the land, was included in the mission of Joshua; and his advanced age supplied a special reason for entering on the immediate discharge of that duty; namely, of allocating Canaan among the tribes of Israel--not only the parts already won, but those also which were still to be conquered. <div eID="gen2822" type="x-p"/>
entries.2dea222b7c5abfe0d1090527a9c6992d6728db25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2105"/><div sID="gen2823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2105"/><hi type="bold">2-6. This is the land that yet remaineth--</hi>that is, to be acquired. This section forms a parenthesis, in which the historian briefly notices the districts yet unsubdued; namely, first, the whole country of the Philistines--a narrow tract stretching about sixty miles along the Mediterranean coast, and that of the Geshurites to the south of it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8">1Sa 27:8</reference>). Both included that portion of the country "from Sihor, which is before Egypt," a small brook near El-Arish, which on the east was the southern boundary of Canaan, to Ekron, the most northerly of the five chief lordships or principalities of the Philistines. <div eID="gen2823" type="x-p"/>
entries.11ff559d1047b5a070ff631fb43a5ae830f560cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2110"/><div sID="gen2835" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2110"/><hi type="bold">8. With whom--</hi>Hebrew, "him." The antecedent is evidently to Manasseh, not, however, the half-tribe just mentioned, but the other half; for the historian, led, as it were, by the sound of the word, breaks off to describe the possessions beyond Jordan already assigned to Reuben, Gad, and the half of Manasseh (see on <reference osisRef="Num.32.1">Nu 32:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.32.33">Nu 32:33</reference>; also see <reference osisRef="Deut.3.8-Deut.3.17">De 3:8-17</reference>). It may be proper to remark that it was wise to put these boundaries on record. In case of any misunderstanding or dispute arising about the exact limits of each district or property, an appeal could always be made to this authoritative document, and a full knowledge as well as grateful sense obtained of what they had received from God (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.6">6</reference>). <chapter eID="Josh.13"/>

entries.c9d6cd388893cda8803898b2625dce9bae5ab0ef: <div eID="gen7886" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen7887" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7888" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7888" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7887" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7889" type="x-p"/> Joshua being old, the Lord informs him of the land yet remaining to be possessed, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.1">Jos 13:1</reference>. Of the unconquered land among the Philistines, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.2">Jos 13:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference>. Among the Canaanites, Sidonians, and Amorites, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.4">Jos 13:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.5">Jos 13:5</reference>. The inhabitants of the hill country and the Sidonians to be driven out, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.6">Jos 13:6</reference>. The land on the east side of Jordan, that was to be divided among the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.7-Jos.13.12">Jos 13:7-12</reference>. The Geshurites and the Maachathites not expelled, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.13">Jos 13:13</reference>. The tribe of Levi receive no inheritance, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.14">Jos 13:14</reference>. The possessions of Reuben described, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.15-Jos.13.23">Jos 13:15-23</reference>. The possessions of Gad, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.24-Jos.13.28">Jos 13:24-28</reference>. The possessions of the half tribe of Manasseh, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.29-Jos.13.31">Jos 13:29-31</reference>. Recapitulation of the subjects contained in this chapter, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.32">Jos 13:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.33">Jos 13:33</reference>. <div eID="gen7889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7890" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen7890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7891" type="x-p"/> Joshua was old - He is generally reputed to have been at this time about a hundred years of age: he had spent about seven years in the conquest of the land, and is supposed to have employed about one year in dividing it; and he died about ten years after, aged one hundred and ten years. It is very likely that he intended to subdue the whole land before he made the division of it among the tribes; but God did not think proper to have this done. So unfaithful were the Israelites that he appears to have purposed that some of the ancient inhabitants should still remain to keep them in check, and that the respective tribes should have some labor to drive out from their allotted borders the remains of the Canaanitish nations. <div eID="gen7891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7892" type="x-p"/> There remaineth yet very much land to be possessed - That is, very much when compared with that on the other side Jordan, which was all that could as yet be said to be in the hands of the Israelites.
entries.a1c20d3b8ef3122ee37868e2de252a25c5fdc02e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen7892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7893" type="x-p"/> The borders of the Philistines, and all Geshuri - The borders of the Philistines may mean the land which they possessed on the sea-coast, southwest of the land of Canaan. There were several places named Geshuri, but that spoken of here was probably the region on the south of Canaan, towards Arabia, or towards Egypt. - Calmet. Cellarius supposes it to have been a country in the vicinity of the Amalekites.
entries.b9db2f24003eb75f4dac5ad109384ca11ef96e62: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen7893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7894" type="x-p"/> From Sihor, which is before Egypt - Supposed by some to be the Pelusiac branch of the Nile, near to the Arabian Desert; called also the river of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Num.34.5">Num 34:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.18">Jer 2:18</reference>. On this subject an intelligent friend favors me with the following opinion: - "The river Sihor is supposed by some to be the Nile, or a branch of it. Others think it the same as what is frequently called the river of Egypt, which lay before or towards the borders of Egypt; which arose out of the mountains of Paran, and ran westward, falling into that bay of the Mediterranean which lies south of the land of the Philistines. This river is often mentioned as the boundary of the Israelites to the southwest, as Euphrates, the great river, was on the northeast. "There was a desert of considerable distance between what is called the river of Egypt and the isthmus of Suez. Solomon reigned to the borders of Egypt, i.e., to this desert; but not in Egypt, nor to the river Nile. "Upon the whole, (though there are difficulties in the matter), I incline to think that the river in question was not the Nile. Sihor (black) might, from some circumstances, be applied to another river as well as the Nile; though some places in Isaiah and Jeremiah seem to restrict it to the Nile." - J. C. <div eID="gen7894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7895" type="x-p"/> Ekron northward - Ekron was one of the five lordships of the Philistines, and the most northern of all the districts they possessed. Baal-zebub, its idol, is famous in Scripture; see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.2">2Kgs 1:2</reference>, etc. The five lordships of the Philistines were Gaza, Ashdod, Askalon, Gath, and Ekron. There is no proof that ever the Israelites possessed Ekron; though, from <reference osisRef="Jos.15.11">Jos 15:11</reference>, some think it was originally given to Judah, but the text does not say so; it only states that the border of the tribe of Judah went out Unto the Side of Ekron. From <reference osisRef="Jos.19.43">Jos 19:43</reference>, we learn that it was a part of the lot of Dan, but it does not appear to have been possessed by any of those tribes. <div eID="gen7895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7896" type="x-p"/> Counted to the Canaanite - It is generally allowed that the original possessors of this country were the descendants of Canaan, the youngest son of Ham. The Philistines sprang from Mizraim, the second son of Ham, and, having dispossessed the Avim from the places they held in this land, dwelt in their stead. See <reference osisRef="Gen.10.13">Gen 10:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.14">Gen 10:14</reference>. <div eID="gen7896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7897" type="x-p"/> Five lords of the Philistines - These dynasties are famous in the Scriptures for their successful wars against the Israelites, of whom they were almost the perpetual scourge. <div eID="gen7897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7898" type="x-p"/> Also the Avites - These must not be confounded with the Hivites. The Avites seem to have been a very inconsiderable tribe, who dwelt in some of the skirts of Palestine. They had been originally deprived of their country by the Caphtorim; and though they lived as a distinct people, they had never afterwards arrived to any authority.
entries.2552edcf842df36aa0e6515497daf517bd21621b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen7898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7899" type="x-p"/> The land of the Canaanites - This lay on the south of the country of the Philistines, towards the sea-coast. <div eID="gen7899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7900" type="x-p"/> Mearah - Supposed to be the city Maratha, on the Mediterranean Sea. - Calmet. Or the river Majora, which falls into the Mediterranean Sea, between Sidon and Berytus. See Pliny, Hist. Nat. lib. v., c. 20. <div eID="gen7900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7901" type="x-p"/> Aphek - See on <reference osisRef="Jos.12.18">Jos 12:18</reference> (note). <div eID="gen7901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7902" type="x-p"/> To the borders of the Amorites - Though the term Amorite is sometimes used to designate the inhabitants in general of the land of Canaan, yet it must be considered in a much more restricted sense in this place. As no Amorites are known to have dwelt in this quarter, Calmet supposes we should read Aramites or Syrians. Joshua, says he, proceeds from Sidon to Aphek, a city of Syria, between Heliopolis and Babylon where was the temple of the Venus of Aphek, and which is spoken of in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.26">1Kgs 20:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.17">2Kgs 13:17</reference>, as the capital of the kings of Syria. From this Joshua passes on to the frontiers of the Syrians, towards Gebal or Gabala, which, according to Ptolemy, was situated in Phoenicia. This conjecture of Calmet is not supported by any authority either from the ancient versions or MSS. Houbigant, however, approves of it: the emendation is simple as it consists in the interchange of only two letters in the same word, הארמי haarammi, for האמרי haemori.
entries.99171b85be028c1c85967800213284d68a0b7eaa: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen7902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7903" type="x-p"/> The land of the Giblites - This people dwelt beyond the precincts of the land of Canaan, on the east of Tyre and Sidon. See <reference osisRef="Eze.27.9">Eze 27:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.83.7">Psa 83:7</reference>; their capital was named Gebal. See Dodd. <div eID="gen7903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7904" type="x-p"/> All Lebanon - See on <reference osisRef="Jos.11.17">Jos 11:17</reference> (note).
entries.1e8ce8a425c8fd9e9173e99204c74beb7b658908: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen7904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7905" type="x-p"/> Misrephoth-maim - See on <reference osisRef="Jos.11.7">Jos 11:7</reference> (note). <div eID="gen7905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7906" type="x-p"/> These will I drive out - That is, if the Israelites continued to be obedient; but they did not, and therefore they never fully possessed the whole of that land which, on this condition alone, God had promised them: the Sidonians were never expelled by the Israelites, and were only brought into a state of comparative subjection in the days of David and Solomon. Some have taken upon them to deny the authenticity of Divine revelation relative to this business, "because," say they, "God is stated to have absolutely promised that Joshua should conquer the whole land, and put the Israelites in possession of it." This is a total mistake. <div eID="gen7906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7907" type="x-p"/> 1. God never absolutely, i.e., unconditionally, promised to put them in possession of this land. The promise of their possessing the whole was suspended on their fidelity to God. They were not faithful, and therefore God was not bound by his promise to give them any part of the land, after their first act of national defection from his worship. <div eID="gen7907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7908" type="x-p"/> 2. God never said that Joshua should conquer the whole land, and give it to them; the promise was simply this: "Thou shalt bring them into the land, and thou shalt divide it among them:" both of which he did, and procured them footing by his conquests, sufficient to have enabled them to establish themselves in it for ever. <div eID="gen7908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7909" type="x-p"/> 3. It was never said, Thou shalt conquer it all, and then divide it; no. Several of the tribes, after their quota was allotted them, were obliged to drive out the ancient inhabitants. See on <reference osisRef="Jos.11.18">Jos 11:18</reference> (note).
entries.b4371bbfb79444d55cb7ee9a9912d966bb9b7dbd: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen7909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7910" type="x-p"/> The nine tribes, and the half tribe of Manasseh - The other half tribe of Manasseh, and the two tribes of Reuben and Gad, had got their inheritance on the other side of Jordan, in the land formerly belonging to Og king of Bashan, and Sihon king of the Amorites.
entries.a20c0ad12cdb0ef079aa21c94db2e7029b8e0e35: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen7910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7911" type="x-p"/> From Aroer - See on <reference osisRef="Jos.12.2">Jos 12:2</reference> (note).
entries.fe043437b3e48915a64a391e907acfda54d5152e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen7911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7912" type="x-p"/> Border of the Geshurites - See on <reference osisRef="Jos.12.5">Jos 12:5</reference> (note).
entries.4cb4a1378a0ff703f15afa605fda7ac84569f935: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen7912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7913" type="x-p"/> Bamoth-baal - The high places of Baal, probably so called from altars erected on hills for the impure worship of this Canaanitish Priapus.
entries.4feb00fb4fa73f1da0dea962886c490bab50ead9: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen7913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7914" type="x-p"/> Jahaza - A city near Medeba and Dibon. It was given to the Levites, <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.78">1Chr 6:78</reference>. <div eID="gen7914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7915" type="x-p"/> Kedemoth - Mentioned <reference osisRef="Deu.2.26">Deu 2:26</reference>; supposed to have been situated beyond the river Arnon. <div eID="gen7915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7916" type="x-p"/> Mephaath - Situated on the frontiers of Moab, on the eastern part of the desert. It was given to the Levites, <reference osisRef="Jos.21.37">Jos 21:37</reference>.
entries.13bb5d42ecf4561ea2ef6a06b8587104a92a7937: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen7916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7917" type="x-p"/> Kirjathaim - This city, according to Eusebius, was nine miles distant from Medeba, towards the east. It passed from the Emim to the Moabites, from the Moabites to the Amorites, and from the Amorites to the Israelites, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.6">Gen 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.2.20">Deu 2:20</reference>. Calmet supposes the Reubenites possessed it till the time they were carried away by the Assyrians; and then the Moabites appear to have taken possession of it anew, as he collects from <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1">Jer 48:1</reference> etc., and <reference osisRef="Eze.25.9">Eze 25:9</reference> etc. <div eID="gen7917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7918" type="x-p"/> Sibmah - A place remarkable for its vines. See <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Isa 16:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jer 48:32</reference>. <div eID="gen7918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7919" type="x-p"/> Zareth-shahar, in the mount of the valley - This probably means a town situated on or near to a hill in some flat country.
entries.27f67bb774a8f751f1ed9817a97ede0635ca5ddf: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen7919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7920" type="x-p"/> Beth-peor - The house or temple of Peor, situated at the foot of the mountain of the same name. See <reference osisRef="Num.25.3">Num 25:3</reference>.
entries.1de0fb307a53fc0122a540287579bad28bf6c13d: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen7920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7921" type="x-p"/> The princes of Midian - See the history of this war, <reference osisRef="Num.31.1">Num 31:1</reference>, etc.; and from that place this and the following verse seem to be borrowed, for the introduction of the death of Balaam here seems quite irrelevant.
entries.35b766df19302d0cc617d052c137add7bc37998d: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen7921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7922" type="x-p"/> The cities and the villages - By villages, חצרים chatserim, it is likely that moveable villages or tents are meant, such as are in use among the Bedouin Arabs; places where they were accustomed to feed and pen their cattle.
entries.d1988433f9674fff19c13bbb9e8787a5b7ee5f5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen7922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7923" type="x-p"/> Half the land on the children of Ammon - This probably was land which had been taken from the Ammonites by Sihon, king of the Amorites, and which the Israelites possessed by right of conquest. For although the Israelites were forbidden to take the land of the Ammonites, <reference osisRef="Deu.2.37">Deu 2:37</reference>, yet this part, as having been united to the territories of Sihon, they might possess when they defeated that king and subdued his kingdom.
entries.e8fb4b9a24a95e6632b7b56bc147d3418720b33d: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen7923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7924" type="x-p"/> Ramath-mizpeh - The same as Ramoth-gilead. It was one of the cities of refuge, <reference osisRef="Jos.20.8">Jos 20:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.4.47">Deu 4:47</reference>. <div eID="gen7924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7925" type="x-p"/> Mahanaim - Or the two camps. Situated on the northern side of the brook Jabbok, celebrated for the vision of the two camps of angels which Jacob had there; see <reference osisRef="Gen.32.2">Gen 32:2</reference>.
entries.d11d41efbd276ee71db756fb96db98f5010f7d38: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen7925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7926" type="x-p"/> Beth-aram - This city was rebuilt by Herod, and called Livias, in honor of Livia, the wife of Augustus. Josephus calls it Julias, Julia being the name which the Greeks commonly give to Livia. - Calmet. <div eID="gen7926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7927" type="x-p"/> Succoth - A place between Jabbok and Jordan where Jacob pitched his tents, from which circumstance it obtained its name, see <reference osisRef="Gen.33.17">Gen 33:17</reference>.
entries.68867c09cfacf5ef3ad33cd06a0cddf9dc88d6da: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen7927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7928" type="x-p"/> The half tribe of Manasseh - When the tribes of Reuben and Gad requested to have their settlement on the east side of Jordan, it does not appear that any part of the tribe of Manasseh requested to be settled in the same place. But as this tribe was numerous, and had much cattle, Moses thought proper to appoint one half of it to remain on the east of Jordan, and the other to go over and settle on the west side of that river.
entries.86eb770f75296847b6b2aa4e8654f76a91cd6990: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen7928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7929" type="x-p"/> The towns of Jair - These were sixty cities; they are mentioned afterwards, and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.21">1Chr 2:21</reference>, etc. They are the same with the Havoth-jair mentioned <reference osisRef="Num.32.41">Num 32:41</reference>. Jair was son of Segub, grandson of Esron or Hezron, and great-grandson of Machir by his grandmother's side, who married Hezron of the tribe of Judah. See his genealogy, <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.21-1Chr.2.24">1Chr 2:21-24</reference>.
entries.d7bb4e47206f555af314a5435f9f92030a824118: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen7929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7930" type="x-p"/> Which Moses did distribute - Moses had settled every thing relative to these tribes before his death, having appointed them to possess the territories of Og king of Bashan, and Sihon king of the Amorites. For particulars on this chapter, the reader, if he judge it of consequence, may consult Calmet.  <chapter eID="Josh.13"/> <div eID="gen7930" type="x-p"/>

entries.55b80023f58a5f9de27da380401d1a9ad9edd722: <div eID="gen2835" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-ms">II. Division of the Land of Canaan Among the Tribes of Israel - Joshua 13-24</title> <div sID="gen2836" type="x-p"/> The distribution of the conquered land among the Israelites is introduced by the command of the Lord to Joshua to enter upon this work, now that he was old, although different portions of land were still unconquered (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.1-Josh.13.7">Jos 13:1-7</reference>); and to this there is appended a description of the land on the east of the Jordan which had already been conquered and divided among the two tribes and a half (Josh 13:8-33). The distribution of the land on this side among the nine tribes and a half is related in its historical order; so that not only are the territories assigned by lot to the different tribes described according to their respective boundaries and towns, but the historical circumstances connected with the division and allotting of the land are also introduced into the description. These historical accounts are so closely connected with the <hi type="italic">geographical</hi> descriptions of the territory belonging to the different tribes, that the latter alone will explain the course pursued in the distribution of the land, and the various ways in which the different territories are described (see the remarks on <reference osisRef="Josh.14.1">Jos 14:1</reference>). For example, in the account of the inheritance which fell to the lot of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, not only are the boundaries most carefully traced, but the towns are also enumerated one by one (Josh 15 and Josh 18:11-28); whereas in the tribe of Joseph (Ephraim and half Manasseh) the list of the towns is altogether wanting (<reference osisRef="Josh.16.1-Josh.16.10">Jos 16:1-10</reference> and 17); and in the possessions of the other tribes, either towns alone are mentioned, as in the case of Simeon and Dan (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.1-Josh.19.9">Jos 19:1-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.19.40-Josh.19.48">Jos 19:40-48</reference>), or the boundaries and towns are mixed up together, but both of them given incompletely, as in the case of Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.10-Josh.19.16">Jos 19:10-16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.19.17-Josh.19.23">Jos 19:17-23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.19.24-Josh.19.31">Jos 19:24-31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.19.32-Josh.19.39">Jos 19:32-39</reference>). This incompleteness, particularly in the territories of the tribes mentioned last, may be explained from the fact, that in northern Canaan there were still very many tracts of land in the hands of the Canaanites, and the Israelites had not acquired a sufficiently exact or complete knowledge of the country, either through Joshua’s campaign in the north, or through the men who were sent out to survey the northern land before it was divided (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.4-Josh.18.9">Jos 18:4-9</reference>), to enable them to prepare a complete account of the boundaries and towns at the very outset. In the same way, too, we may explain the absence of the list of towns in the case of the tribes of Ephraim and half Manasseh-namely, from the fact that a large portion of the territory assigned to the tribe of Joseph was still in the possession of the Canaanites (vid., <reference osisRef="Josh.17.14-Josh.17.18">Jos 17:14-18</reference>); whilst the omission of any account of the boundaries in the case of Simeon and Dan is attributable to the circumstance that the former received its inheritance within the tribe of Judah, and the latter between Judah and Ephraim, whilst the space left for the Danites was so small, that Ephraim and Judah had to gave up to them some of the town in their own territory. Thus the very inequality and incompleteness of the geographical accounts of the possessions of the different tribes decidedly favour the conclusion, that they are the very lists which were drawn up at the time when Joshua divided the land. There is nothing to preclude this supposition in the fact that several towns occur with different names, e.g., <hi type="italic">Beth-shemesh</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ir-shemesh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.10">Jos 15:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.41">Jos 19:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.16">Jos 21:16</reference>), <hi type="italic">Madmannah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Beth-marcaboth</hi>, <hi type="italic">Sansanna</hi> and <hi type="italic">Hazar-susa</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.31">Jos 15:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.5">Jos 19:5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Shilchim</hi> and <hi type="italic">Sharuchen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.32">Jos 15:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.6">Jos 19:6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Remeth</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jarmuth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.21">Jos 19:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.29">Jos 21:29</reference>), or in other smaller differences. For variations of this kind may be sufficiently explained from the fact that such places were known by two different names, which could be used promiscuously; whilst in other cases the difference in the name amounts to nothing more than a different mode of writing or pronouncing it: e.g., <hi type="italic">Kattah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kartah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.15">Jos 19:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.34">Jos 21:34</reference>), <hi type="italic">Eshtemoh</hi> and <hi type="italic">Eshtemoa</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.50">Jos 15:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.14">Jos 21:14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Baalah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Balah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.29">Jos 15:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.3">Jos 19:3</reference>); or simply in the contraction of a composite name, such as <hi type="italic">Ramoth</hi> in Gilead for <hi type="italic">Ramoth-mizpeh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.36">Jos 21:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.26">Jos 13:26</reference>); <hi type="italic">Bealoth</hi> and <hi type="italic">Baalath-beer</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.24">Jos 15:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.8">Jos 19:8</reference>), <hi type="italic">Lebaoth</hi> and <hi type="italic">Beth-lebaoth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.32">Jos 15:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.6">Jos 19:6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Hammath</hi> and <hi type="italic">Hammoth-dor</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.35">Jos 19:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.32">Jos 21:32</reference>). <div eID="gen2836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2837" type="x-p"/> If the author, on the other hand, had drawn from later sources, or had simply given the results of later surveys, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes, there can be no doubt that much greater uniformity would be found in the different lists.<note placement="foot">The arguments employed by <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> in support of his assertion, consist on the one had of inconclusive and incorrect assertions, and are founded on the other hand upon arbitrary assumptions. In the first place, for example, he asserts that “a large number of towns are omitted from the lists, which were within the boundaries mentioned and were in existence in the very earliest times, viz., <hi type="italic">in the south</hi>, Tamar (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.7">Gen 14:7</reference>), Arad (Num 21:1), Atbach, Rachal, Aroer, and Siphamoth (1Sa 30:28.), Gerar (Gen. 20:26); <hi type="italic">in the Shephelah</hi>, Gaza, Askalon, Gath, Ashdod, Jabne, and Joppa (see Jos 15:45.); in <hi type="italic">Benjamin</hi>, Michmash and Nob (1Sa 13:2., <reference osisRef="Josh.22.19">Jos 22:19</reference>); in the <hi type="italic">north</hi>, Aphek, Lassaron, Madon, Shimron-meron, and Merom (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.5">Jos 11:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.12.18-Josh.12.20">Jos 12:18-20</reference>), as well as Meroz and Ajjalon (Jdg 5:23; Jdg 12:12); and these with other places would assuredly not be wanting here, if Joshua and his associates had distributed the towns as well as the land, and furnished our author with the lists.” But it would be difficult to bring forward the proofs of this, since <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> himself acknowledges that there are gaps in the lists which have come down to us, some of which can be proved to be the fault of the copyists, - such, for example, as the want of a whole section after <reference osisRef="Josh.15.19">Jos 15:19</reference> and Jos 21:35. Moreover, the Philistine towns of Ashdod and Gaza are really mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.46">Jos 15:46</reference>, and the others at all events hinted at; whereas <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> first of all arbitrarily rejects <reference osisRef="Josh.15.45-Josh.15.47">Jos 15:45-47</reference> from the text, in order that he may afterwards be able to speak of it as omitted. Again, with many of the places mentioned as omissions, such as Atbach, Rachal, Siphamoth, etc., it is very questionable whether they were towns at all in Joshua’s time, or, at all events, such towns as we should expect to find mentioned. And lastly, not only are no catalogues of towns given at all in the case of Ephraim and Manasseh, but we have only imperfect catalogues in the case of Zebulun, Asher, and Naphtali; and, as we have already observed, this incompleteness and these gaps can be satisfactorily explained from the historical circumstances under which the allotment of the land took place. <hi type="italic">Secondly</hi>, <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> also maintains, that “Joshua’s conquests did not extend to the Lebanon (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.4-Josh.13.5">Jos 13:4-5</reference>), and yet the author mentions towns of the Asherites there (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.28">Jos 19:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.19.30">Jos 19:30</reference>): Bethel was not taken till after the time of Joshua (Jdg 1:22.), and this was also the case with Jerusalem (Jdg 1:8), and in the earliest times of the judges they had no Hebrew inhabitants (Jdg 19:12), yet the author speaks of both places as towns of the Benjamites (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.22">Jos 18:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.28">Jos 18:28</reference>); Jericho and Ai were lying in ruins in Joshua’s time (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.24">Jos 6:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.8.28">Jos 8:28</reference>), yet they are spoken of here as towns of Benjamin that had been rebuilt (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.21">Jos 18:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.23">Jos 18:23</reference>); it is just the same with Hazor in Naphtali (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.13">Jos 11:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.36">Jos 19:36</reference>); and according to Jdg 1:1, Jdg 1:10., Hebron and Debir also were not conquered till after Joshua’s time.” But all this rests (1) upon the false assumption, that the only towns which Joshua distributed by lot among the tribes of Israel were those which he permanently conquered, whereas, according to the command of God, he divided the whole land among the Israelites, whether it was conquered or not; (2) upon the erroneous opinion, that the towns which had been destroyed, such as Jericho, Ai, and Hazor, were allotted to the Israelites as “rebuilt,” whereas there is not a word about this in the text. It is just the same with the arguments used by <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> in proof of the composition of Josh 13-21 from three different documents. The material discrepancies have been forced upon the text, as we shall see when we come to an explanation of the passages in question; and the verbal differences prove nothing more than that the geographical account of the boundaries and towns contains no allusion to the priesthood, to sacrifice, or to certain other things which no one would think of looking for here.</note> <div eID="gen2837" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">COMMAND OF GOD TO DIVIDE THE LAND OF CANAAN. DESCRIPTION OF THE TERRITORY OF THE TWO TRIBES AND A HALF. — CHAP. XIII.</title> <div sID="gen2838" type="x-p"/> Introduction to the Division of the Land. - <reference osisRef="Josh.13.1">Jos 13:1</reference>-7. Command of the Lord to Joshua to distribute the land of Canaan by lot among the nine tribes and a half. <reference osisRef="Josh.13.1">Jos 13:1</reference> contains only the commencement of the divine command; the conclusion follows in Jos 13:7. <reference osisRef="Josh.13.2-Josh.13.6">Jos 13:2-6</reference> form a parenthesis of several clauses, defining the last clause of <reference osisRef="Josh.13.1">Jos 13:1</reference> more fully. When Joshua had grown old, the Lord commanded him, as he was advanced in years, and there was still much land to be taken, to divide “<hi type="italic">this land</hi>,” i.e., the whole of the land of Canaan, for an inheritance to the nine tribes and a half, and promised him at the same time that He would drive out the Canaanites from those portions of the land that were not yet conquered (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.6">Jos 13:6</reference>). The words “<hi type="italic">grown old and come into years</hi>” (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.24.1">Gen 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.11">Gen 18:11</reference>, etc.) denote advanced age in its different stages up to the near approach of death (as, for example, in <reference osisRef="Josh.23.1">Jos 23:1</reference>). Joshua might be ninety or a hundred years old at this time. The allusion to Joshua’s great age serves simply to explain the reason for the command of God. As he was already old, and there still remained much land to be taken, he was to proceed to the division of Canaan, that he might accomplish this work to which he was also called before his death; whereas he might very possibly suppose that, under existing circumstances, the time for allotting the land had not yet arrived. -  In <reference osisRef="Josh.13.2-Josh.13.6">Jos 13:2-6</reference> the districts that were not yet conquered are enumerated separately.
entries.d42d391f95b0c8cde842933c34a034ea5e88dc7a: <reference osisRef="Josh.13.2-Josh.13.4">Jos 13:2-4</reference> <div eID="gen2838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2839" type="x-p"/> All the <hi type="italic">circles of the Philistines</hi> (<hi type="italic">geliloth</hi>, circles of well-defined districts lying round the chief city). The reference is to the five towns of the Philistines, whose princes are mentioned in Jos 13:3. “<hi type="italic">And all Geshuri:</hi>” not the district of Geshur in Peraea (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.11">Jos 13:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.13">Jos 13:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.12.5">Jos 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">Deu 3:14</reference>), but the territory of the Geshurites, a small tribe in the south of Philistia, on the edge of the north-western portion of the Arabian desert which borders on Egypt; it is only mentioned again in 1Sa 27:8. The land of the Philistines and Geshurites extended from the Sichor of Egypt (on the south) to the territory of Ekron (on the north). <hi type="italic">Sichor</hi> (<hi type="italic">Sihor</hi>), lit. the black river, is not the Nile, because this is always called היאר (the river) in simple prose (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.1">Gen 41:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.3">Gen 41:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.1.22">Exo 1:22</reference>), and was not “before Egypt,” i.e., to the east of it, but flowed through the middle of the land. The “<hi type="italic">Sichor before Egypt</hi>” was the brook (<hi type="italic">Nachal</hi>) of Egypt, the Ῥινοκοροῦρα, the modern Wady <hi type="italic">el Arish</hi>, which is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.4">Jos 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.47">Jos 15:47</reference>, etc., as the southern border of Canaan towards Egypt (see at Num 34:5). <hi type="italic">Ekron</hi> (Ἀρρακών, lxx), the most northerly of the five chief cities of the Philistines, was first of all allotted to the tribe of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.11">Jos 15:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.45">Jos 15:45</reference>), then on the further distribution it was given to Dan (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.43">Jos 19:43</reference>); after Joshua’s death it was conquered by Judah (Jdg 1:18), though it was not permanently occupied. It is the present Akîr, a considerable village in the plain, two hours to the south-west of Ramlah, and on the east of Jamnia, without ruins of any antiquity, with the exception of two old wells walled round, which probably belong to the times of the Crusaders (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. iii. p. 23). “<hi type="italic">To the Canaanites is reckoned</hi> (the territory of the) <hi type="italic">five lords of the Philistines</hi>,” i.e., it was reckoned as belonging to the land of Canaan, and allotted to the Israelites like all the rest. This remark was necessary because the Philistines were not descendants of Canaan (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.10.14">Gen 10:14</reference>), but yet were to be driven out like the Canaanites themselves as being invaders of Canaanitish territory (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.2.23">Deu 2:23</reference>). סרני, from סרן, the standing title of the princes of the Philistines (vid., Jdg 3:3; Jdg 16:5.; <reference osisRef="1Sam.5.8">1Sa 5:8</reference>), does not mean kings, but princes, and is interchangeable with שׂרים (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.6">1Sa 29:6</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.4">1Sa 29:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.9">1Sa 29:9</reference>). At any rate, it was the native or Philistian title of the Philistine princes, though it is not derived from the same root as <hi type="italic">Sar</hi>, but is connected with <hi type="italic">seren</hi>, <hi type="italic">axis rotae</hi>, in the tropical sense of <hi type="italic">princeps</hi>, for which the Arabic furnishes several analogies (see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> Thes. p. 972). <div eID="gen2839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2840" type="x-p"/> The capitals of these five princes were the following. <hi type="italic">Azzah</hi> (<hi type="italic">Gaza</hi>, i.e., the strong): this was allotted to the tribe of Judah and taken by the Judaeans (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.47">Jos 15:47</reference>; Jdg 1:18), but was not held long. It is at the present time a considerable town of about 15,000 inhabitants, with the old name of Ghazzeh, about an hour from the sea, and with a seaport called <hi type="italic">Majuma</hi>; it is the farthest town of Palestine towards the south-west (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. ii. pp. 374ff.; <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvi. pp. 35ff.; <hi type="italic">Stark</hi>, Gaza, etc., pp. 45ff.). <hi type="italic">Ashdod</hi> (Ἄζωτος, <hi type="italic">Azotus</hi>): this was also allotted to the tribe of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.46-Josh.15.47">Jos 15:46-47</reference>), the seat of Dagon-worship, to which the Philistines carried the ark (1Sa 5:1.). It was conquered by Uzziah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.6">2Ch 26:6</reference>), was afterwards taken by Tartan, the general of Sargon (<reference osisRef="Isa.20.1">Isa 20:1</reference>), and was besieged by Psammetichus for twenty-nine years (<hi type="italic">Herod.</hi> ii. 157). It is the present <hi type="italic">Esdud</hi>, a Mahometan village with about a hundred or a hundred and fifty miserable huts, upon a low, round, wooded height on the road from Jamnia to Gaza, two miles to the south of Jamnia, about half an hour from the sea (vid., <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> i. p. 368). <hi type="italic">Ashkalon</hi>: this was conquered by the Judaeans after the death of Joshua (Jdg 1:8-9); but shortly afterwards recovered its independence (vid., Jdg 14:19; <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.17">1Sa 6:17</reference>). It is the present <hi type="italic">Askulân</hi> on the sea-shore between Gaza and Ashdod, five hours to the north of Gaza, with considerable and widespread ruins (see v. Raum. pp. 173-4; <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, xvi. pp. 69ff.). <hi type="italic">Gath</hi> (Γέθ): this was for a long time the seat of the Rephaites, and was the home of Goliath (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.22">Jos 11:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.4">1Sa 17:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.23">1Sa 17:23</reference>; 2Sa 21:19.; 1Ch 20:5.); it was thither that the Philistines of Ashdod removed the ark, which was taken thence to Ekron (<reference osisRef="1Sam.5.7-1Sam.5.10">1Sa 5:7-10</reference>). David was the first to wrest it from the Philistines (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">1Ch 18:1</reference>). In the time of Solomon it was a royal city of the Philistines, though no doubt under Israelitish supremacy (1Ki 2:39; 1Ki 5:1). It was fortified by Rehoboam (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.8">2Ch 11:8</reference>), was taken by the Syrians in the time of Joash (2Ki 12:18), and was conquered again by Uzziah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.6">2Ch 26:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.2">Amo 6:2</reference>); but no further mention is made of it, and no traces have yet been discovered<note placement="foot">According to the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> <hi type="italic">Geth</hi>), it was a place five Roman miles from Eleutheropolis towards Diospolis, whereas <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> (on Mic 1) says: “<hi type="italic">Gath</hi> was near the border of Judaea, and on the road from Eleutheropolis to Gaza; it is still a very large village;” whilst in the commentary on Jer 25 he says: “Gath was near to and conterminous with Azotus,” from which it is obvious enough that the situation of the Philistine city of Gath was altogether unknown to the Fathers. <hi type="italic">Hitzig</hi> and <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> suppose the Βαιτογάβρα of <hi type="italic">Ptolemy</hi> (5:16, 6), <hi type="italic">Betogabri</hi> in <hi type="italic">Tab. Peuting</hi>. ix. e. (the Eleutheropolis of the Fathers, and the present <hi type="italic">Beit Jibrin</hi>, a very considerable ruin), to be the ancient Gath, but this opinion is only founded upon very questionable etymological combinations; whereas <hi type="italic">Thenius</hi> looks for it on the site of the present <hi type="italic">Deir Dubban</hi>, though without any tenable ground.</note> (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 420, and <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, Pal. pp. 191-2). “<hi type="italic">And the Avvites</hi> (Avvaeans) <hi type="italic">towards the south</hi>.” Judging from <reference osisRef="Deut.2.23">Deu 2:23</reference>, the <hi type="italic">Avvim</hi> appear to have belonged to those tribes of the land who were already found there by the Canaanites, and whom the Philistines subdued and destroyed when they entered the country. They are not mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.10.15-Gen.10.19">Gen 10:15-19</reference> among the Canaanitish tribes. At the same time, there is not sufficient ground for identifying them with the Geshurites as <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> does, or with the Anakites, as <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> has done. Moreover, it cannot be decided whether they were descendants of Ham or Shem (see <hi type="italic">Stark</hi>. Gaza, pp. 32ff.). מתּימן (<hi type="italic">from</hi>, or on, <hi type="italic">the south</hi>) at the commencement of <reference osisRef="Josh.13.4">Jos 13:4</reference> should be attached to <reference osisRef="Josh.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference>, as it is in the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate, and joined to העוּים (the Avvites). The Avvaeans dwelt to the south of the Philistines, on the south-west of Gaza. It gives no sense to connect with the what follows, so as to read “<hi type="italic">towards the south all the land of the Canaanites;</hi>” for whatever land to the south of Gaza, or of the territory of the Philistines, was still inhabited by Canaanites, could not possibly be called “all the land of the Canaanites.” If, however, we were disposed to adopt the opinion held by <hi type="italic">Masius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>, and understand these words as relating to the southern boundaries of Canaan, “the possessions of the king of Arad and the neighbouring petty kings who ruled in the southern extremity of Judaea down to the desert of Paran, Zin, Kadesh,” etc., the fact that Arad and the adjoining districts are always reckoned as belonging to the Negeb would at once be decisive against it (compare Jos 15:21. with <reference osisRef="Josh.10.40">Jos 10:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.11.16">Jos 11:16</reference>, also Num 21:1). Moreover, according to <reference osisRef="Josh.10.40">Jos 10:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.21">Jos 10:21</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Josh.11.16-Josh.11.17">Jos 11:16-17</reference>, Joshua had smitten the whole of the south of Canaan from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza and taken it; so that nothing remained unconquered there, which could possibly have been mentioned in this passage as not yet taken by the Israelites. For the fact that the districts, which Joshua traversed so victoriously and took possession of, were not all permanently held by the Israelites, does not come into consideration here at all. If the author had thought of enumerating all these places, he would have had to include many other districts as well. <div eID="gen2840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2841" type="x-p"/> Beside the territory of the Philistines on the south-west, there still remained to be taken (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.4">Jos 13:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.5">Jos 13:5</reference>) in the north, “<hi type="italic">all the land of the Canaanites</hi>,” i.e., of the Phoenicians dwelling on the coast, and “<hi type="italic">the caves which belonged to the Sidonians unto Aphek</hi>.” <hi type="italic">Mearah</hi> (the cave) is the present <hi type="italic">Mugr Jezzin</hi>, i.e., cave of Jezzin, on the east of Sidon, in a steep rocky wall of Lebanon, a hiding-place of the Druses at the present time (see at Num 34:8; also <hi type="italic">F. v. Richter</hi>, Wallfahrten in Morgenland, p. 133). <hi type="italic">Aphek</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Aphik</hi>, was allotted to the tribe of Asher (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.30">Jos 19:30</reference>; Jdg 1:31); it was called Ἄφακα by the Greeks; there was a temple of Venus there, which Constantine ordered to be destroyed, on account of the licentious nature of the worship (<hi type="italic">Euseb</hi>. Vita Const. iii. 55). It is the present <hi type="italic">Afka</hi>, a small village, but a place of rare beauty, upon a terrace of Lebanon, near the chief source of the river <hi type="italic">Adonis</hi> (<hi type="italic">Nahr Ibrahim</hi>), with ruins of an ancient temple in the neighbourhood, surrounded by groves of the most splendid walnut trees on the north-east of Beirut (see <hi type="italic">O</hi>. <hi type="italic">F. v. Richter</hi>, pp. 106-7; <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. p. 663; and <hi type="italic">V. de Velde</hi>, Reise. ii. p. 398). “<hi type="italic">To the territory of the Amorites:</hi>” this is obscure. We cannot imagine the reference to be to the territory of Og of Bashan, which was formerly inhabited by Amorites, as that did not extend so far north; and the explanation given by <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, that farther north there were not Canaanites, but Amorites, who were of Semitic origin, rests upon hypotheses which cannot be historically sustained.
entries.b0323ec111382fae91e213490c8484ee73c26d7b: <reference osisRef="Josh.13.5-Josh.13.7">Jos 13:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen2841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2842" type="x-p"/> There still remained to be taken (2) “<hi type="italic">the land of the Giblites</hi>,” i.e., the territory of the population of Gebal (1Ki 5:18; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.9">Eze 27:9</reference>), the <hi type="italic">Byblos</hi> of the classics, on the Mediterranean Sea, to the north of Beirut, called <hi type="italic">Jebail</hi> by the Arabs, and according to <hi type="italic">Edrisi</hi> (<hi type="italic">ed. Jaubert</hi>, i. p. 356), “a pretty town on the sea-shore, enclosed in good walls, and surrounded by vineyards and extensive grounds planted with fruit trees” (see also <hi type="italic">Abulfed</hi>. Tab. Syr. p. 94).
